learn.title: You can now update the tools in an existing session in the Agents API public beta.
learn.headline: OpenAI agent sessions now compact old context in the background by default.
learn.reason: Shows how agents trim context and why that can raise token costs, which you're studying next.

card.headline: OpenAI agents can now get new tools mid-session
card.gist: An agent is an AI model that can take actions, called tools. OpenAI now lets you change those tools during a running conversation, called a session.
card.picture: It's like saving a new version of a spreadsheet tab over the old one. You don't add rows to it; you replace the whole tab. Anything you leave out is gone.
card.why_you: If you build agents on OpenAI, send the full tool list each time you change it. If you send only the new tool, all the others are removed.
card.remember: Changing tools mid-session? Send the full list, every time.
card.term_meaning: Actions an agent is allowed to take, such as calling your own function or searching the web.
card.say_it: OpenAI's Agents API lets me change an agent's tools mid-session. Each update replaces the whole list.
card.follow_up_why: Because the update overwrites the old list instead of merging, so any tool left out is dropped.
card.reality_check: This is from OpenAI's own changelog, for a public beta (test) version. Trying it needs OpenAI API access.
card.try_it: Read OpenAI's 'Configuring Agents' docs page. Note when each kind of tool change takes effect.

learn.title: Random Is Almost Enough? Stable and Low-Cost Benchmark Compression via BestRand
learn.headline: Random benchmark subsets usually work but sometimes give large errors; BestRand fixes it.
learn.reason: Shows why small eval subsets mislead and how to sample safely; uses your stats background.

card.headline: Testing AI models on a small random subset is almost enough
card.gist: AI models are scored on big fixed sets of test questions, called benchmarks. A new paper shows a small random subset usually gives a close score, but sometimes misses badly.
card.picture: It's like estimating a big table's average from a random sample of rows. Most samples land close to the true average. Now and then, one sample lands far off.
card.why_you: You will score models on a budget, often on a subset of questions. Plan for the rare subset that gives a misleading score.
card.remember: A random sample is usually close; plan for rare big misses.
card.term_meaning: Scoring a model on a small subset of a benchmark that closely matches the full benchmark's score.
card.say_it: Random subsets usually estimate the full benchmark score well. The risk is a rare subset with a large error.
card.follow_up_why: Because the error across subsets is long-tailed: most errors are small, but a few are much larger.
card.reality_check: These are the authors' own results, not independent tests. Their code and data are free on GitHub.
card.try_it: With any scored test set, draw 1,000 random 10% subsets. Plot how far each subset's score lands.

learn.title: Building a Multi-Agent System from Scratch: Architecture Patterns
learn.headline: Three ways to structure multi-agent systems: pipeline, orchestrator, blackboard
learn.reason: Agent architecture patterns with an example; common interview topic you're learning.

card.headline: A builder explains when to split AI work across several agents
card.gist: An agent is an AI model that can use tools and choose its next step. The advice: start with one agent, and split the work only when it clearly helps.
card.picture: One Python script can run a whole ETL job. You split it into separate jobs when steps need different setups, can run in parallel, or need testing alone. Each split adds a handoff that can break.
card.why_you: You plan to learn agent loops next. Every extra agent adds more model calls, more cost and new ways to fail.
card.remember: Start with one agent. Split only when a part clearly needs it.
card.term_meaning: Several AI agents, each with a narrower job, passing work between them, for example in a fixed order or through a lead agent.
card.say_it: I start with one agent, and split when parts need different instructions or tools, parallel runs, or separate tests.
card.follow_up_why: Because every extra agent adds model calls, cost and new ways to fail, like bad data passed along as fact.
card.reality_check: This is one author's experience from their own projects, not an independent study. You can try the ideas for free with local models.
card.try_it: Pick a task you know well. Ask: can I write its steps as a fixed checklist? If yes, a fixed-order pipeline fits.
